title: The Savoy Male and Female College
text:

The next spring the family bought a home in Savoy and had lived there two or three months when the terrible tornado swept away three-quarters of Savoy, only leaving intact a small part of the village. The morning after the catastrophe, while waiting for the T. and F. B. R. to repair a broken rail, I, following some newspaper instinct, issued what might be called as a "special edition" of the paper for which I was working a circular giving all the information I could get about the storm. My hours of deep anxiety about my parents were soon eased by news from them, and I was soon again at work, glad that they were safe and unhurt.

I soon gave up my job in Sherman and joined my family in Savoy for the purpose of attending school. The school had been chartered a few months previous to the tornado, and could therefore be styled a legal institution of learning, but was not officially raised to the rank of a college until two years later, when it was chartered as a college. During the entire first session after the charter was issued, I was on hand and, enthusiastic student and good one. I attended the first college year without the loss of a day, but unfortunately my father died the second year, and the family was looking to me for support; money was failing, and I had to help make a living for the family. He died in May, 1882, leaving my mother and sister; then on I had to support my mother and sister and put my little sisters through college. When Mr. P. W. Halsel had heard of my circumstances, he was very graciously insistent that I go on to school and forget about the immediate money needs—help in later failure as I felt to study to repay. With nature and these kind encouragements I still attended, though by necessity of part-time work it took me until 1889 to wear today; so I had to get out and go to work. It was only by the kindly help of Mr. Halsel that I was able to round out the full requirements for the B.S. During the seven years in which I was working for an education, I taught in about six different schools of four, five, and eight months respectively; in addition to this I pursued a course in penmanship in my spare hours, helped survey land one summer in the fall, cut cord wood in winter, and taught penmanship at odd hours, and I had one year of six paying teachers in class work.
